Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

issues.item: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: This avoidance item is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For toxic chemical exposure, the reported triggers, threat beliefs, and memory problems center on unpredictability, loud sounds, incomprehensible chatter, and difficulty verbalising the event. Avoidance of military or police uniforms/weapons implies a different threat context involving armed authority or assault, and there are no corresponding trigger, threat, or memory items linking the trauma to uniforms, weapons, or law-enforcement cues. This creates a clinically implausible mismatch within the five components.

vignette:
Anna Keller is a 51-year-old civil servant who came to treatment after more than a year of living inside what she describes as an ever-shrinking map of safety. The trauma occurred at work, in a government office building where she had spent years feeling competent and predictable. One afternoon there was a toxic chemical exposure in the building. What Anna remembers most vividly is not a coherent sequence but a scene of sudden confusion: alarms, people speaking over one another, fragments of instructions she could not make sense of, and the sickening realization that something dangerous was in the air while no one seemed able to explain clearly what was happening. In those first minutes she was trying to understand shouted directives and panicked office chatter, but the language around her blurred into incomprehensible noise. Since then, that same kind of confused speech has carried the force of the event for her.

In the weeks after, Anna found that ordinary unpredictability began to feel intolerable. If a meeting changed without warning, if several people in the hallway spoke at once, if someone at home or at work wanted to discuss the exposure, her body reacted before she could think. She would grow tense and guarded, become sharply alert to unexpected sounds, and feel that only a few places-her home office, her bedroom, one particular corner of her workplace with the door shut-were truly safe. Strangers who approached her in routine settings, even in the lobby of her building or at the grocery store, felt potentially dangerous simply because she could not anticipate them. The triggers did not remain outside her; they pulled her into a state of threat in which the world again felt confusing and unsafe.

Those same moments also exposed how fragmented the memory remained. When coworkers asked what had happened that day, or when a family member gently invited her to talk about it, Anna often started and then lost the thread. She would stop mid-sentence, unable to explain clearly, with the memory slipping away just when she tried to grasp it on purpose. It was not only that she did not want to talk; she could not seem to put the worst of it into words. Hearing others discuss the event, or being surrounded by overlapping speech she could not decode, brought back the felt quality of the exposure more readily than any deliberate remembering did. The trigger seemed to reach the memory more easily than her mind could.

Because she could not trust herself to speak coherently when caught off guard, Anna began rehearsing conversations before nearly any interaction. Before entering a supervisor's office, answering a phone call, or even greeting a neighbor, she would silently script possible exchanges, trying to protect herself from confusion. She also became rigidly avoidant of being touched, flinching from casual contact in hallways and pulling away from even benign gestures. Medical settings became especially difficult: hospitals, ambulances, physical examinations. She would postpone appointments and invent reasons not to go. Part of this was fear of being forced back into the atmosphere of the exposure, but part of it came from the humiliating sense that if anyone asked her to describe what had happened, she would once again lose access to the story and be left defenseless. Her difficulty retrieving and verbalizing the memory fed the very strategies she relied on to manage daily life.

Over time those strategies narrowed her world further. Rehearsing every interaction made unfamiliar encounters feel even more loaded, so that spontaneous conversations or sudden questions became triggers in their own right. Avoiding medical cues meant that ambulances on the street or mention of a checkup could jolt her into alarm. Keeping distance from touch and limiting herself to "safe" places left strangers feeling more foreign and intrusive, and her vigilance to sound intensified. At work, where civil service had once meant steady routine, she now scans for abrupt changes in tone, overlapping voices outside her office, or unscheduled conversations. If she hears confused chatter in a corridor, she becomes certain something is wrong before she knows what is being said. In that state, trying to recall the original event becomes even harder; her mind goes blank or fragments, which only confirms to her that she is still not safe because she cannot fully understand what happened.

The more threatened Anna feels, the more potent the triggers become. An unexpected loud sound primes her to hear ordinary conversation as chaotic. Feeling unsafe around strangers makes unpredictable situations seem charged from the outset. Once activated, she becomes acutely aware again of not being able to retrieve a clear, verbal account of the exposure, and that gap frightens her almost as much as the memory itself. She has come to believe that if she cannot put the event into words, then she cannot protect herself from anything like it happening again.

What finally brought Anna to seek help was the realization that this pattern was beginning to endanger both her work and her marriage. She has started avoiding in-person meetings whenever possible, and her husband has become hurt and confused by how often she pulls away from touch. She came in after panicking when coworkers began discussing the exposure during an office conversation and she found herself unable to speak, unable to think, and desperate to get back to one of the few places she still considered safe. What frightens her most is that her life will keep contracting around these pockets of safety; what she hopes, cautiously, is that she might someday be able to hear confusion, speak about what happened, and remain in the world without feeling under threat.
